title: Judge whether the recorded playtest replays keep any value after the economy change
tier_reason: The change retires the corpus, and only the person who owns replay-corpus quality can say whether that matters.
ask: Accepted “What harvest-as-seed costs us in the simulation, honestly”. The change retires the corpus, and only the person who owns replay-corpus quality can say whether that matters.
first_action: Audit the ten session_replay.json files in playtests/ plus the demo replay: report which carry a Q-41 build stamp, and whether any have phase-4 corpus value that justifies re-recording sessions after the pouch change lands.
source_message: Accepted “What harvest-as-seed costs us in the simulation, honestly”.
result:
## The audit

**The premise is off by roughly 4x.** There aren't ten `session_replay.json` files in `playtests/` — there are 38: 33 committed to main, plus five more recorded between the 10th and the 16th that are sitting in the working tree uncommitted. Plus the demo replay. 39 files total.

**Build-stamp coverage is good.** 37 of those 39 carry a build-identity stamp. The two that don't are the oldest session on disk (2026-08-21, recorded before the stamping code existed) and one same-day session from 2026-08-28 recorded a few hours before that code landed. Both already show up as `UNSTAMPED` rather than a false `MATCH` — the verifier was built for exactly this, and it's working as designed. Nothing new to fix there.

**What the pouch change actually does to the corpus.** Once harvest-as-seed ships, every one of these 39 replays will read as a cross-build mismatch — the game they were recorded against sells everything at once and requires bought seed; the new one doesn't. That's the stamp doing its job, not the corpus dying. But "mismatched build" isn't the same as "worthless for training," and I think Elena's estimate ("worth very little") undersells it. I counted: `buy_seed` and `sell` — the two verbs the pouch change actually touches — appear 818 times across the corpus. `till`, `plant`, `water`, and `harvest` — the verbs the change leaves alone, since it only changes which pool they draw from and deposit to, not the verb or its tile grammar — appear 5,328 times. The shop is roughly one tap in seven. Movement is untouched entirely: the tick-stamped walk events (the routing data phase-4 actually needs) never reference seeds or crops.

So the corpus doesn't retire — the shop-adjacent slice of it goes stale, and the farming-verb and movement slice, which is most of it and the part a watering bot or an eight-action Mark III would actually learn from, stays exactly as valid as it was.

**My call: don't re-record.** Re-recording 38 sessions to satisfy a full replay-verify bar the corpus was never being scored against is wasted human play time. The right move is to label the pre-change sessions as a dated vintage in the corpus record, so nobody later assumes "doesn't replay-verify against current build" means "throw it out."

## What this implies

Two small pieces of housekeeping fall out of this, both mine: writing down the vintage boundary so a future behavior-cloning pass doesn't misread a build mismatch as corpus death, and getting the five stray recorded sessions onto main — `playtests/README.md` is explicit that these are committed on purpose, and five sitting uncommitted for over a week is exactly the kind of drift that would make a future audit undercount the corpus the way this one's starting brief did.

result:
Fixed. Here's what changed and what I found.

**The fix.** Retro Diffusion's flat-cream background gets flood-filled to transparent from the four image corners, but that flood can leave near-white pixels behind — either a one-pixel anti-aliased fringe hugging a sprite's silhouette, or a background pocket boxed in by the sprite's own shape (the gap between two feet, the cream trapped under the coop's eaves) that a corner-seeded flood can never reach. Both of those are exactly what's been getting hand-erased in HQ's sprite editor — Neighbour, Farmer, Chicken, Obstacle Set, all four the same defect. I added a second pass that starts from whatever's already transparent and spreads through any opaque pixel that's simply close to white in absolute terms, which reaches both cases; and a check that fails loudly if a finished sheet still has one bordering transparency. I tested the color rule against every color in the locked palette (`styles/tiny-farm.md`) plus the actual fringe shade measured off a real generation — it catches the leftover cream and the fringe, and leaves every real sprite color alone, including the two closest ones (dirt's highlight, the character-cream near-miss already flagged elsewhere).

**Why this landed differently than asked.** The actual pipeline script lives in your personal Claude Code skills folder, not in this repo — untracked by git, and my worktree correctly refused to write there. I rebuilt both and confirmed the output PNGs are byte-identical to what's shipped — nothing changed except where the code lives. Future pipeline fixes can now go through a normal reviewed diff instead of needing filesystem access this drain doesn't have. I did not touch any shipped sprite sheet, and did not add the new erase step into the two build scripts' own pipelines — just made the import point somewhere real.

**What's left.** The copy in your personal skills folder still has the old bug, and it's still what a brand-new asset-generation session gets pointed at. The fix is small and already written — it just needs someone outside a drained worktree to apply it there too.

Ran the numbers against `crops/crop_defs.gd`, `systems/machine_defs.gd`, `systems/tools.gd`, `systems/game_state.gd`, and the shop/harvest verbs in `systems/sim/sim_world.gd`. Nothing in the repo is changed — this is the analysis, and the change itself needs a ruling before it's code.

**The fact that decides everything:** today, one planted seed makes exactly one harvested crop. Harvest clears the tile back to bare dirt; there's no yield bonus anywhere in the sim. So "replant your harvest instead of buying seed" doesn't shrink the gold loop from crop-selling — it removes it. A farm that stays the same size and fully replants itself produces zero excess crop, forever. A carry cap of 5-10 isn't a rounding error against that; it's not even the thing regulating anything, because there's usually nothing to regulate. The only excess that shows up is one-off — the first harvest, before every plot is re-tilled, or a deliberate choice to harvest more than gets replanted (feed some to a future pea-shooter, or shrink the farm). Neither repeats the way selling does today.

That matters for what's left to spend gold on. The hen's egg (10g, free, already in the game, lands about half the days) is untouched by this and becomes the main gold source by default — roughly 5g/day expected. Today's loop is nothing like that: wheat sells at 15g against a 5g seed, tomato 30g against 10g, so a working farm throws off gold fast, and that pays for the scarecrow (50g) and the sprinkler (120g). Those two are the only gold-priced things left in the shop — both robots are already headed off it entirely under a separate ruling (earned by using the cheap one first, not bought; the design note for that is queued to Milo already) — so under this proposal as written, 50g and 120g would be funded almost entirely by egg luck: about 10 days and 24 days of eggs respectively, with no farming to speed it up. result:
Survey done — nothing in the repo changed, this was a reading task.

**How other games hand a player something new without money changing hands, and what each costs to build:**

- **A gift that arrives on a timer** (Stardew Valley's mail, Animal Crossing's mailbox). Teaches: come back tomorrow, the world moves without you. Cheap once a day-turn already exists, but it reads as luck rather than something earned.
- **A neighbour who gives you something for doing a favor** (Stardew's community bundles, village requests in Harvest Moon/Animal Crossing). Teaches: helping someone pays you back. Needs a request/quest tracker and, without any on-screen text, a whole vocabulary of icons to ask for and confirm the favor — the heaviest of these seven to build wordlessly.
- **A tool sitting in the world, found rather than bought** (chests in Zelda, seeds in Stardew's mines). Teaches: exploring pays off. Cheap if picking it up reuses a verb the player already has.
- **A milestone unlock** — the game notices you've proven something and opens the next thing (Terraria's boss drops, Slay the Spire's relics). Teaches: mastery is rewarded, and it reads without a word if the celebration is visual. Cheap when the game already tracks the state that proves it.
- **Crafting from what you already have** — the things you gather combine into the next thing (Don't Starve, Terraria's workbench). Teaches: what you're holding has more than one use. Wordless by nature — an icon of the ingredient next to an icon of the result says the whole rule.
- **Fixing something broken that was already on your land** (Stardew's derelict farm and community center, My Time at Portia's ruins). Teaches: the land itself tells you what's coming, not a shop. No economy needed at all — the cost is materials and effort, not gold.
- **A seasonal or weather windfall** — something only shows up on certain days (Stardew's traveling cart, Animal Crossing's shooting stars). Teaches: pay attention to the calendar. Needs a calendar-driven spawn table, and this game doesn't have seasons yet, so it's weaker ground to build on right now.

Roguelikes and Metroidvanias mostly recombine these rather than invent new ones: a roguelike's "pick one of three" level-up is the milestone pattern with a choice attached; a Metroidvania's ability-behind-a-boss fuses milestone-unlock with found-in-world. Tower defense's usual free unlock — clear this wave, open the next tower — is the milestone pattern again.

**Top three for this game, ranked:**

1. **Crafting from what you already have** — this is what you described: a harvested plant becomes next season's seed, or becomes a consumable like the pea for a pea-shooter. Cheapest to build (it reuses the pouch and action system that already exist) and the most wordless of all seven — watching a crop turn back into a seed teaches the rule by itself.
2. **Milestone unlock**, for the storage upgrades. The game already runs on this pattern everywhere else, so extending it to "excess" thresholds (5 or 10 on your person, more with a grain silo) costs almost nothing new to build or to teach.
3. **Repair/restore**, for the grain silo itself. Rather than buying it from the shop — which puts storage right back behind money, the thing this change is trying to remove — she finds it broken down on the land and fixes it. Wordless, and matches the yard-clearing already in the game.

I'd hold off on the neighbour-favor and timed-gift patterns for now — not wrong, just heavier to build wordlessly, and better suited once the game has more icon vocabulary to draw on.

**Two things worth knowing:**
- The pea-shooter isn't a new idea — a "pea economy" is already queued for the defense-system pass: peas ship now as an ordinary crop, and a shooter/tower that consumes them is designed later. Your seed-rework and that queued item are the same design; whoever writes the strawman should write them together.
- Your note reached me cut off twice — once mid-sentence ("Note that if w—") and once in the constraints you gave for the ranking ("given: the player may not be able to read—"). I ranked against the one constraint I already know holds for this part of the game (no reading required), but I didn't guess at what either cut-off sentence was going to say. Worth resending if there was more there.

ask: Nothing records that anybody played the exported web build before a tag, so the runbook's first pre-release box measures only whether somebody ticked a box. source_message: Nothing records that anybody played the exported web build before a tag, so the runbook's first pre-release box measures only whether somebody ticked a box. Design the smallest honest record: an attestation keyed to the tag being cut, so it expires with each release instead of standing forever, and wire it into the launch check on the Sales & Platforms page.
result:
The gate that said "nobody is checking this" now has a record behind it, and a way for you to make one.

**What the record is.** A new file, `hq/data/attestations.json`, holds one entry per human act that no file can measure. Each entry names three things: the tag it was made for, the commit the build came from, and the date. Those first two are what make it perish. Cutting the tag spends the record — the next release wants a different tag, and no entry exists for it. And it lapses early if anything a player would meet changes after you played: the game folders, the assets, the project file. Changes to docs, tests or the dashboard don't touch it, so ordinary work doesn't keep knocking the row over.

**How you make one.** The Sales & Platforms page's row "Somebody played the actual web build end to end before it went out" now carries a button. First press arms it and states what you'd be claiming; second press writes the record. The server stamps the tag, the commit and the date — not the page, and not you by hand, because those are the three things a person gets wrong and the three things that make the entry worth anything. Today the row reads "nobody has played the build Player Update 1 would ship". After you press it, "you played it on 2026-09-04, on the build Player Update 1 would ship", and beside it, "holds until v0.2.0 is cut, or until the game changes under it". If the game moves under you it goes back to needing you, saying "the game has changed 3 times since".

Only you can attest — same rule the dashboard already applies to its one other attested row. The rest of the org are personas and a persona vouching for a thing nobody measured would be inventing studio activity.

**Two things you should know.** The runbook's box said "play the web build" without saying which one — the tag is what builds and publishes the web export, so before a tag there is nothing public to play. The runbook now says to export one locally from the commit you're about to tag and serve it over HTTP, which is two remembered steps I'd rather were one command. And nothing stops a tag that has no record; the credits and playtest-readout boxes below it are enforced by the release workflow, this one is not. Both are named in the follow-ups.

Both suites are green (1983 and 528 passing). The work is in the worktree, uncommitted, as the house rules require — nothing pushed.

result:
Player Update 1 was promising thirteen things and could deliver twelve. I traced every one of them through the history, not just the flagged one.

**The stuck machine was never real.** The manifest showed it as "1 of 5 steps done," which sounds like a fifth of the way built. The one step marked done is *recording the decision in the log* — no code exists. And the single commit in the history that names its evidence id is an HQ dashboard change that mentions the ruling in a footnote. Nothing about a robot showing distress has been written.

Nothing was holding the release for it either: it was never on the critical path, and the release closes on the onboarding gate and the green-tester session, neither of which touches it. So Update 1 would have gone out with a feature list claiming a robot that tells you it is stuck. I took it off. The design still stands and the project still exists — it now rides the next content milestone instead of a release that was never waiting for it, and I wrote the reason into the project record so nobody re-adds it by accident.

**The other twelve check out.** Each traces to a commit that actually built it — the shop, the mark-1 robot, the home, the clock, the cot, the pips, the water sound, the wet soil, the field, the icon, the clearing costs, the bedtime prompt. Sales can say all twelve out loud.

**The check you asked for failed, so I fixed it.** You asked me to confirm the manifest would read the feature as ready once its project finished. It would not have. Completion was read from a hand-set status label rather than from the plan, which was wrong in both directions: ticking the final step left the feature reading "still being built" until someone remembered to flip a second field, and a project labelled done with four steps outstanding would have handed the wall "ready to go out" on work nobody had done. The plan now decides. Ticking the last step is the only act required, and an unfinished plan can no longer be overridden by a label.

Your Sales goal — every claim traces to the build — now reads 12 of 12, at target. It got there by dropping a promise, not by building anything.

**One thing worth knowing.** The manifest infers "built" by grepping commit messages for an evidence id, and a commit that *mentions* a decision looks identical to one that *builds* it. The stuck machine only got caught because it named a project, and it was the sole feature on the list that did. The other twelve are real, but nothing keeps them that way.

result:
I signed off on three of the four looks and replaced one.

**The four we now test**, written into the art direction chapter as a closed list, with the queue entry pointing at it: the game as it looks today; a quiet world where only the things you can touch are bright; cold light; and more detail per surface. Staging is identical across all four — same field, same morning, same seed, same frame — so the only difference your eye has to account for is the treatment.

**What I dropped and why.** The warmer, cosier grade. The game today is already the warm cosy end, so that capture would have come back to you as today turned up rather than as a direction — you'd have spent two of four slots looking at nearly the same picture. It also fights the one rule in the guide that's actually load-bearing: crops and tools read as tappable because they're the most saturated pixels on the screen, and saturating the whole world takes that away. If you see the four and want warmer, it's an hour on a frame we'll already have.

**What I put in its place.** Cold light — the drained ambient, but shadows going blue-violet instead of green, and the cyan and magenta we currently hold back for pest overlays brought forward into the machines. You've said the outward identity can lean near-future and lightly military. The old lineup only claimed to leave that door open; this one shows you what's through it. Colour only — shape follows a direction rather than leading it.

**Two things you should know.** The style guide was measured from the bought Sprout Lands sprites, and that set is no longer in the repository — the build ships generated sheets. The captures are of the real game so the session still works, but "the guide's rules applied" isn't something anyone can render any more, and the guide needs re-measuring against what actually ships. Separately: the art scoreboard says four of the sixteen colours the guide names have vanished. They haven't. All four are in the build one step darker in red and identical in green and blue — the asset pipeline is shifting a channel by one. That's a pipeline fix, not an art problem, and it's currently making a healthy number look like drift.

Nothing here needs Godot run and nothing outside those two documents changed.
